one_sentence: This paper argues that sin spreads through communities according to the same SIR model dynamics as infectious diseases, with R₀ determining epidemic or containment.
executive_summary: This document establishes a structural isomorphism between epidemiology (the SIR model of infectious disease spread) and Christian hamartiology (the social propagation of sin). The core claim is that sin spreads through communities according to the same population dynamics as infectious diseases: susceptible individuals become fallen at a rate proportional to contact with fallen individuals (β), and fallen individuals are restored at a rate γ. The epidemic threshold R₀ = β/γ determines whether sin spreads exponentially (R₀ > 1) or is contained (R₀ < 1). The mapping yields ten independent correspondences, including super-spreaders (leadership sin), quarantine (church discipline), herd immunity (community holiness threshold), and asymptomatic carriers (hidden sin). Biblical authors used contagion language (leaven, root of bitterness) consistent with this structure. The isomorphism is bidirectional: epidemiology constrains viable community health strategies, and theology predicts threshold effects and super-spreading dynamics confirmed by network epidemiology. The conclusion is that purely individualistic sanctification models fail in high-exposure environments; community-level strategies addressing transmission dynamics are necessary.
short_summary: This document is a structural isomorphism mapping the SIR epidemiological model onto the social propagation of sin in Christian theology. The core claim is that sin spreads through communities according to the same population dynamics as infectious diseases, with R₀ = β/γ determining whether sin becomes epidemic or is contained. Key evidence includes ten independent correspondences (super-spreaders, quarantine, herd immunity, asymptomatic carriers) and biblical authors' use of contagion language (leaven, root of bitterness). This matters because it predicts that purely individualistic sanctification models fail in high-exposure environments and that community-level strategies addressing transmission dynamics are necessary for moral health.
